name: Ohtahara syndrome
aliases: early infantile developmental and epileptic encephalopathy with burst-suppression

reference.source: ILAE classification / Nelson Textbook of Paediatrics
clinicalPearls: Onset is very early, usually within the first weeks to three months of life, with frequent tonic spasms occurring both awake and asleep
The defining EEG hallmark is a burst-suppression pattern present in both wakefulness and sleep
Causes are heterogeneous, including structural brain malformations and pathogenic variants in genes such as STXBP1, KCNQ2, SCN2A and ARX
Development is severely impaired from onset, and seizures are typically drug-resistant
It may evolve into West syndrome and later into Lennox-Gastaut syndrome as the child grows
Structural imaging is essential because malformations of cortical development are a frequent underlying cause
Distinguishing it from early myoclonic encephalopathy rests on the predominant seizure type and the state-dependence of the EEG pattern
reference.pathophysiology: Ohtahara syndrome is an early infantile developmental and epileptic encephalopathy in which severe disruption of neuronal networks in the immature brain produces continuous epileptic activity. The underlying causes, whether structural malformations of cortical development or pathogenic variants affecting synaptic transmission and ion channels, converge on profound cortical hyperexcitability and impaired inhibition. This generates the persistent burst-suppression pattern and frequent tonic spasms, while the same widespread dysfunction arrests brain development from the outset.
additionalDifferentials: Inborn errors of metabolism presenting with neonatal seizures
additionalInvestigations: EEG demonstrating burst-suppression in both wakefulness and sleep
Brain MRI to detect malformations of cortical development and structural lesions
Epilepsy gene panel or exome sequencing (e.g. STXBP1, KCNQ2, SCN2A, ARX)
Metabolic workup including trials of vitamin-responsive causes such as pyridoxine
CSF studies where a metabolic or neurotransmitter disorder is suspected
redFlags: Refractory tonic spasms with persistent burst-suppression in early infancy
Failure to respond to pyridoxine trial when a vitamin-responsive cause is possible
Evidence of a progressive metabolic disorder
reference.prognosis: The prognosis is generally very poor, with high early mortality, severe intellectual and motor disability in survivors, and frequent evolution to West and then Lennox-Gastaut syndrome. Outcome is strongly influenced by the underlying cause.
pitfalls: Failing to trial vitamin-responsive treatments before concluding refractoriness
Overlooking a subtle malformation of cortical development on early imaging
Confusing it with early myoclonic encephalopathy by not characterising the predominant seizure type
Not pursuing genetic testing, which increasingly identifies a specific cause
management: Treat any identifiable underlying cause, including a trial of pyridoxine, pyridoxal phosphate and folinic acid for vitamin-responsive seizures and targeted therapy where a metabolic cause is found
Antiseizure medication to reduce seizure burden, such as phenobarbital, vigabatrin, sodium valproate or zonisamide, acknowledging frequent drug resistance
Tailor treatment to the genetic cause, for example sodium-channel blockers such as carbamazepine or oxcarbazepine in KCNQ2-related disease
Consider the ketogenic diet, and resective epilepsy surgery where a focal structural lesion is identified
Adrenocorticotropic hormone or corticosteroids if the disorder evolves into West syndrome with epileptic spasms
Supportive and developmental care: feeding and respiratory support, physiotherapy and management of severe neurodevelopmental impairment
Multidisciplinary paediatric neurology, metabolic and genetics input with early palliative care and family support given the poor prognosis
Genetic counselling and gene testing (STXBP1, KCNQ2, SCN2A, ARX) to define recurrence risk
